idiom_name: Object.freeze + private class fields + copy-on-write factories
implementation_notes: JavaScript has no immutability declaration, so a value type is built from one shallow primitive plus conventions: private class fields (or closures) keep the state out of reach, Object.freeze makes the instance's own properties non-writable and non-configurable, and updates are functions or methods that spread the old state into a new object. Freeze is shallow, so nested objects must be private or frozen too; in sloppy-mode code a write to a frozen object fails silently, which is why the factory that freezes should be the only construction path.
pitfalls: Object.freeze is shallow and does not touch nested objects: a frozen wrapper can still expose a mutable array or object, so deepFreeze is a case-by-case pattern with cycle handling (a function's prototype refers back to the function).
In non-strict code, writes to a frozen object fail silently instead of throwing, so the defect surfaces far from its cause; class bodies and modules are strict, where the write throws a TypeError.
Object spread copies one level: { ...state, nested } shares nested references, so a later mutation of the nested object is visible through both the old and the new value.

variants.name: Immutable.js persistent collections with structural sharing
variants.implementation_notes: Where values are large and updated often, freezing copies too much: Immutable.js provides persistent List, Map, Set and Record types whose mutating-looking methods (set, update, push) return a new collection that shares the unchanged structure, so an update costs O(log n) instead of O(n). Records give a fixed key set with defaults; comparisons must use Immutable.is or equals because the collections are values rather than identities, and withMutations batches several updates before freezing.
pitfalls: A persistent collection is only as immutable as its elements: a Map of plain mutable objects still lets those objects change without the collection noticing.
Value semantics break reference equality: === and React's default shallow comparison no longer detect changes, so consumers must compare with Immutable.is or rely on reference change.
Converting back with toJS() hands out mutable data again, which leaks the discipline at exactly the boundary it was meant to protect.
